Ten anomalies an analyst could test, and when each one fails

Each entry gives a definition in our words, a measurable signal, the data it needs, a condition that weakens it and the passage we checked. Full APA references are under Sources and AI.

Price and calendar pattern. See the Bollinger view

1. Short-term reversal

Definition
Compare shares with recent losses against recent winners over the next few days or weeks
Signal
Relative past short-term return (e.g. prior-week or prior-month return); in our chart, a close outside the 20-session Bollinger Bands
Data needed
Daily, weekly, or monthly adjusted stock prices (and bid-ask quotes)
Weakens when
Bid-ask bounce mimicking reversals, high transaction/turnover costs, and opposing industry momentum; strong trends, as Tesla in October 2021
Evidence
Lehmann (1990), abstract, p. 1: winners and losers in one week show sizable return reversals the next week, and the author reports profits after corrections for bid-ask spreads and transaction costs.
AI note
AI helped draft this row. Its first draft copied the momentum evidence from the example row (Jegadeesh & Titman, 1993), so we replaced it with Lehmann (1990).

Price and calendar pattern.

2. Long-run reversal

Definition
Compare shares with extreme multi-year past losses against extreme multi-year past winners
Signal
Relative past long-term return (e.g. 3- to 5-year cumulative returns)
Data needed
Multi-year historical adjusted stock prices
Weakens when
Very few independent multi-year holding periods, increased risk/distress in past losers, and alternative factor-risk explanations
Evidence
De Bondt & Thaler (1985), abstract, p. 793: thirty-six months after portfolio formation, the past losers earned about 25% more than the past winners. Fama & French (1996) and Chan (1988) for risk-adjusted counter-arguments.
AI note
AI helped draft this row. Team check: the 25% figure in the abstract, and the reference link, which first opened a different paper.

Price and calendar pattern. See the calendar check

3. January effect

Definition
Compare January returns with other months, historically with particular attention to small-capitalization firms
Signal
Calendar month of return & firm market capitalization
Data needed
Historical monthly stock returns sorted by firm size deciles over long sample periods
Weakens when
High transaction costs, bid-ask spread frictions for illiquid small stocks, and distinguishing tax-loss selling from institutional window dressing; in our large-company file January beat the other months in only 4 of 7 years
Evidence
Rozeff & Kinney (1976), abstract, p. 379: mean returns differ across months mainly because of large January returns, except in 1929 to 1940. Haugen & Jorion (1996) for testing persistence and arbitrage limits.
AI note
AI helped draft this row. Team check: the 4 of 7 count, recomputed in the Section 3 code cell.

Price and calendar pattern. See the calendar check

4. Day-of-the-week effect

Definition
Compare close-to-close returns ending on different weekdays
Signal
Calendar day of return (Monday through Friday indicator)
Data needed
Daily adjusted closing stock prices and exchange calendar dates
Weakens when
Friday-to-Monday includes the weekend, exchange calendar differences, sample period dependence, and market/political regime shifts; in our file Monday was the best weekday from 2020 to 2026
Evidence
French (1980), abstract, p. 55: from 1953 to 1977 the average Monday return of the S&P 500 was negative in each five-year subperiod. Cross (1973) and Gibbons & Hess (1981) for early day-of-the-week studies.
AI note
AI helped draft this row. Our data disagreed with French (1980): Monday averaged +0.138% per day, so we added that to the weakness column.

Price and calendar pattern.

5. Pre-holiday effect

Definition
Compare the return immediately before an exchange holiday with the return on ordinary trading sessions
Signal
Pre-holiday trading session indicator
Data needed
Daily stock returns paired with actual exchange closure dates
Weakens when
Limited sample size of pre-holiday trading sessions, single large price moves driving the average, and transaction cost frictions
Evidence
Ariel (1990), abstract, p. 1611: the average pre-holiday return was nine to fourteen times the mean of the other days. Lakonishok & Smidt (1988) for broad seasonal anomaly evidence.
AI note
AI helped draft this row. Team check: the nine to fourteen times figure against the abstract.

Company and news data.

6. Post-earnings-announcement drift

Definition
Compare the returns after earnings announcements that beat expectations with the returns after announcements that missed them
Signal
Standardized unexpected earnings (SUE): actual minus expected earnings, divided by their usual variation
Data needed
Quarterly earnings, announcement dates, an expected value (analyst forecast or the same quarter last year) and daily adjusted prices
Weakens when
Large, widely followed companies where prices react faster, high trading costs in small stocks, and lower returns after the anomaly was published
Evidence
Bernard & Thomas (1989), abstract, p. 1: the drift is more consistent with a delayed price response to earnings news than with a risk premium. McLean & Pontiff (2016), abstract, p. 5, for lower returns after publication.
AI note
Claude drafted this row. Team check: the delayed-response conclusion against the abstract. Our price file has no earnings data, so we did not chart it.

Company and news data.

7. Value

Definition
Compare shares that are cheap relative to their book value with shares that are expensive
Signal
Book-to-market ratio (book equity divided by market value), sorted into groups once a year
Data needed
Book equity with the date it became public, shares outstanding and prices
Weakens when
Long periods when growth stocks lead the market, and lower returns after publication
Evidence
Fama & French (1992), abstract, p. 427: size and book-to-market equity combine to capture the cross-sectional variation in average stock returns. McLean & Pontiff (2016), abstract, p. 5: published predictors earn 58% less after publication.
AI note
Claude drafted this row. Team check: the abstract wording and the 58% figure.

Company and news data.

8. Size

Definition
Compare small companies with large companies by market value
Signal
Market capitalization rank at a date; smallest group against largest group
Data needed
Shares outstanding and prices for many firms, including small ones; our 100-stock file holds only large firms, so it cannot test size
Weakens when
After the early 1980s and after publication, and because the effect is concentrated in very small, illiquid firms
Evidence
Banz (1981), abstract, p. 3: smaller firms had higher risk-adjusted returns than larger firms for at least forty years, and the effect came mainly from very small firms.
AI note
Claude drafted this row from the first words of our draft. We added the note that our file cannot test size.

Company and news data.

9. Profitability

Definition
Compare highly profitable firms with unprofitable firms, measured against their assets
Signal
Gross profits (revenue minus cost of goods sold) divided by total assets
Data needed
Revenue, cost of goods sold and total assets with their release dates, plus prices
Weakens when
In periods when unprofitable growth stocks lead, and when accounting data reaches the market late
Evidence
Novy-Marx (2013), abstract, p. 1: gross profits-to-assets has roughly the same power as book-to-market for predicting average returns, and profitable firms earn significantly higher returns despite higher valuation ratios.
AI note
Claude drafted this row. Team check: the abstract wording.

Company and news data.

10. Disposition effect

Definition
Compare how often investors sell shares with a gain against how often they sell shares with a loss
Signal
Proportion of gains realized minus proportion of losses realized (PGR minus PLR)
Data needed
Account-level trading records with purchase prices and dates; price files cannot measure it
Weakens when
In December, when investors sell losing shares to reduce taxes
Evidence
Odean (1998), abstract, p. 1775: in the records of 10,000 brokerage accounts, investors showed a strong preference for realizing winners rather than losers, and tax-motivated selling was most evident in December.
AI note
Claude drafted this row from the first words of our draft. Team check: the 10,000 accounts and the December result in the abstract.

We carry short-term reversal into Activity 3

We compared the two price patterns from our table that our file can test on its own: short-term reversal (row 1) and the January effect (row 3). Reversal gives a daily signal with hundreds of observations and a clear period when it failed. The January effect gives seven observations, all from large companies.

CriterionShort-term reversal (Bollinger)January effect
SignalA close outside the 20-session Bollinger BandsJanuary return minus the average of the other months
Data in our file1,698 Tesla sessions with bands: 138 short and 85 long signals7 Januaries (2020 to 2026)
What the file shows27 Oct 2026: Tesla closed at $407.46, above its upper band of $399.31January beat the other months in 4 of 7 years
Period of weaknessOctober 2021: 10 short signals while Tesla rose 43.7%2020 to 2022: three Januaries in a row below the other months
Main sourceLehmann (1990)Rozeff & Kinney (1976)
VerdictChosen: clearer signal, more data, an informative failure periodToo few observations to tell luck from a pattern

Plan for Activity 3

We will test a reversal rule on Tesla with a different window from the worked example, for example a 50-session band with two standard deviations. The signal at one close sets the position for the next session, from January 2020 to 30 October 2026. We will compare it with buying and holding Tesla over the same dates from the same starting amount, and state a trading cost per trade.

Why not momentum

The AMD and NVIDIA chart follows the course example row, medium-term momentum. Momentum is not one of our ten entries, so we kept it as the worked illustration of a dated, checked value and did not choose it for Activity 3.
